85.title: The cave of Hira
85.hook: near forty, he climbs to a small cave on a mountain above Mecca to think and pray alone
85.howItsDone: Many Muslims keep a spiritual retreat, i'tikaf, staying in the mosque for the last ten nights of Ramadan; pilgrims to Mecca often climb Jabal an-Nur to see the cave of Hira, though it is not part of the rites.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Stone on a cloak, and every clan lifting together. Your line was everyone takes a corner. Did you find a cloak for your standoff? Day eighty-five.

He has a good life now. A loving wife, children, a solid business, a name everyone trusts. He's nearing forty. And something in him keeps pulling him out of town. A few miles from Mecca there's a steep, rocky mountain. Near the top, tucked between boulders, is a cave. Tiny. Room for a person to sit, maybe to lie down, not much more. And that's where he starts going. Alone. Carrying food and water up the mountain, and staying for days and nights at a time. Not to escape his family; he keeps coming back to them. But to be somewhere quiet enough to think.
screen: `A GOOD LIFE, NEARING FORTY.` → `A STEEP MOUNTAIN, A TINY CAVE.` → `DAYS AND NIGHTS, ALONE.`

segments.voice: The cave is called Hira. The mountain is known today as Jabal an-Nur, the Mountain of Light. The oldest account of this time is a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. She says that before revelation came, he began to have dreams that came true, clear as the break of dawn. And then, in her words as they've come down, solitude was made dear to him. He would go to the cave of Hira and worship there for many nights, then come back to Khadijah for more provisions, and go again. The Arabic word for what he did there is tahannuth: devotion, turning away from wrongdoing, a kind of spiritual retreat. What exactly he prayed, and how, the sources don't say. They tell us where, and for how long, and that he kept going back. Ibn Ishaq adds that he spent a month there every year, and that the month was Ramadan, and that he fed the poor who came to him. Think about what he was pulling away from: a city of idols, of trade and pride, where the poor were ignored and the strong did as they liked. Up there, none of it. Wind, rock, stars, and the city small below. People still climb to Hira today. It's a hard climb, rough steps cut into the mountain, and at the top a narrow gap in the rocks. It isn't part of any required ritual. People go because he went. And because everything that comes next in his life, and in the life of Islam, starts in that small, quiet place.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit somewhere quiet for two minutes. If you can, move. Another room, a stairwell, a parked car, the far corner of a park. Go a little higher or a little further away, if only a few steps. Then sit. Let the noise of the day get small below you, the way Mecca did from the mountain. You don't need to think of anything holy. Just be where nobody needs you for a moment. If you pray, you can simply sit with Allah, without asking for anything. The bell holds the time.
The cave of Hira. A small cave on the Mountain of Light above Mecca, where he went to be alone and pray, night after night.
Your line: go up to the quiet. Today, find one pocket of time and one place where nobody needs you, and use it for nothing but quiet. Tomorrow, the night everything changes. Day eighty-five.

86.title: "Read" in the cave
86.hook: alone in the cave, he is seized by the angel Jibril, who says one word: read
86.howItsDone: Muslims remember the first revelation during Ramadan, especially in the last ten nights when many seek Laylat al-Qadr; many children learn Surah Al-'Alaq as one of their first surahs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave of Hira, a tiny room of rock above Mecca. Your line was go up to the quiet. Did you find a pocket of it? Today, what happened in that quiet. Day eighty-six.

A night in Ramadan. He's in the cave, alone, the way he's been so many nights. And then, suddenly, he isn't alone. Someone is there, the angel Jibril, though he doesn't know that yet, and the angel says one word. Iqra. Read. Recite. And he answers, honestly: I am not a reader. He had never learned to read or write. The angel takes hold of him and squeezes him, hard, until he can't bear it, then lets go. Read. I am not a reader. Again, the crushing grip. Read. Again: I am not a reader. A third time. And then the angel speaks the words he is to recite.
screen: `A NIGHT IN RAMADAN.` → `IQRA. READ.` → `I AM NOT A READER.`

segments.voice: These are the first words of the Qur'an to come down, according to most Muslim scholars. They open Surah Al-'Alaq, the ninety-sixth. In Pickthall's translation: “Read: In the name of thy Lord Who createth, Createth man from a clot. Read: And it is thy Lord the Most Bountiful Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not.” Look at what's inside that. The first word of revelation is a command to read, given to a man who could not read. Iqra comes from the root q-r-', to read, to recite aloud. And from that same root comes the word Qur'an itself: the recitation, the thing that is read aloud. So the first word already names the whole book. Then, in the name of your Lord. Not read anything, anyhow. Read in the name. That's the bismillah from day two of this path, now as the very first instruction. Then who He is: the one who creates, who made the human being from a clinging clot, from almost nothing. And then, twice, the pen. The one who teaches by the pen, who teaches the human being what he did not know. It's striking. A man who couldn't write is given, as his first revelation, a verse about writing and learning. Muslims have taken that seriously for fourteen centuries: libraries, schools, the careful copying of the Qur'an by hand, the idea that seeking knowledge is part of faith. And they remember the night. The Qur'an says it came down in the month of Ramadan, on a night it calls Laylat al-Qadr, the Night of Power, better than a thousand months.
screen: `THE FIRST WORDS TO COME DOWN.` · `IQRA AND QUR'AN: ONE ROOT.` · `IN THE NAME OF THY LORD.` · `WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.` · then, large: `READ, IN THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line slowly, twice. Take any line that matters to you. A verse, a poem, a sentence from a letter. Or use today's: read, in the name of thy Lord who createth. Read it once, at normal speed. Then read it again, far slower, one word at a time, letting each word land before the next. Notice what you missed the first time. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah, the way the first revelation did. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Iqra. Read, or recite: the first word of the Qur'an to be revealed, from the same root as the word Qur'an itself.
Your line: read, in the name. Today, before you read something that matters, pause for one breath and read it on purpose. Tomorrow, he runs down the mountain. Day eighty-six.

87.title: "Cover me"
87.hook: he runs home trembling, and Khadijah wraps him up and reminds him who he is
87.howItsDone: Muslims often quote Khadijah's words, that Allah would never disgrace one who keeps family ties and helps the weak, to encourage someone who is afraid, and honor her as the first to believe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, iqra: the first word of the Qur'an, spoken in a cave to a man who couldn't read. Your line was read in the name. Did you read something on purpose? Day eighty-seven.

Picture him coming down that mountain in the dark. Rough steps, loose stones, his heart pounding so hard he can feel it in his neck and shoulders. Whatever happened up there, he doesn't have words for it yet. He doesn't know if he's losing his mind. He runs the miles back into Mecca, through the door of his house, straight to Khadijah, and says two words, over and over. Zammiluni, zammiluni. Cover me. Wrap me up. Cover me.
screen: `DOWN THE MOUNTAIN IN THE DARK.` → `HIS HEART POUNDING.` → `ZAMMILUNI: COVER ME.`

segments.voice: The hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah, says they wrapped him up until the fear left him. Just that. A blanket, and someone holding it around him. No questions yet. Then he tells Khadijah everything, and says: I'm afraid for myself. Now listen to what she says back. It's one of the most loved answers in all of Islamic history. Never, she says. By Allah, Allah would never disgrace you. And then she gives her reasons, and every one of them is about how he treats people. You keep up your family ties. You carry the burdens of the weak. You give to those who have nothing. You honor your guests. You stand by people when disaster hits them. Think about that. He comes home terrified that something is wrong with him. And she doesn't argue theology. She doesn't explain the angel. She reminds him who he is, from the evidence of how he's lived: a good man is not abandoned by Allah. She was the first to believe him, before there was anything to believe except him. And the moment stayed in the Qur'an itself. Two surahs, the seventy-third and seventy-fourth, open by addressing the Prophet ﷺ as the one wrapped up, al-muzzammil, and the one enfolded in a cloak, al-muddaththir. The blanket from that night became a name. Muslims tell this story to show that the first comfort of Islam came not from a scholar or a crowd, but from a wife at home, holding a blanket and saying: I know you.
screen: `THEY WRAPPED HIM UNTIL THE FEAR LEFT.` · `I'M AFRAID FOR MYSELF.` · `NEVER. SHE LISTS HOW HE LIVES.` · `AL-MUZZAMMIL: THE ONE WRAPPED UP.` · then, large: `ALLAH WOULD NOT DISGRACE YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone who is shaken. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life who's rattled right now. A scare at the doctor. A bad week. A shock they haven't told anyone about. Don't plan a speech. Plan the blanket first: sitting with them, a meal, a call where you just listen. Then think of two or three true things about how they've lived that you could remind them of. If you pray, you can ask Allah to steady them. The bell holds the time.
Cover me. Zammiluni: what he said to Khadijah when he came down from the cave, shaking, and she wrapped him up.

Your line: Allah would not disgrace you. Today, tell someone who's doubting themselves one true thing about how they live. Tomorrow, Khadijah takes him to see an old man who knows the scriptures. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: Waraqa the old cousin
88.hook: Khadijah takes him to her elderly, blind cousin, a man who knew the earlier scriptures, and the old man recognizes what came to him
88.howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Waraqa in the opening chapter of Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is often told to show that the Prophet's message was recognized as belonging to the line of Musa and the earlier prophets.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cover me: Khadijah wrapped him up and reminded him who he was. Your line was Allah would not disgrace you. Did you say one true thing to someone doubting? Day eighty-eight.

When something happens to you that you can't explain, who do you go to? Not the loudest person you know. Usually the oldest one who's read the most. The grandmother who's seen everything. The professor who's retired but still answers the phone. That's what Khadijah does. Once her husband has stopped shaking, she takes his hand and walks him across Mecca to see her cousin. His name is Waraqa. He's very old. He's gone blind. And he's spent his long life studying the scriptures that came before.
screen: `WHO DO YOU GO TO?` → `KHADIJAH'S OLD COUSIN.` → `BLIND, AND DEEPLY READ.`

segments.voice: The same hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari tells it. Waraqa ibn Nawfal had turned away from the idols of Mecca long before, and become a Christian. He could write in Hebrew, and he had copied out from the Gospel as much as Allah willed. Khadijah says: cousin, listen to what your nephew has to say. So the old man asks: nephew, what did you see? And the Prophet ﷺ tells him everything. The cave. The grip. The word. Read. And the old blind man recognizes it at once. He says: this is the Namus that Allah sent down to Musa. The Namus: a word the hadith uses for the angel who carries revelation, the keeper of the divine secret. Muslims understand it as Jibril. So the first person outside the family to hear the story doesn't hear something new and strange. He hears something old: the same messenger who came to Musa. And then he says something heavy. I wish I were young. I wish I could be alive when your people drive you out. And the Prophet asks, surprised: will they drive me out? Yes, Waraqa says. No one has ever brought what you've brought without being opposed. If I live to see that day, I will stand with you with all my strength. But, the hadith says, not long after, Waraqa died. The old man recognized what had come, blessed it, warned of what was coming, and then was gone. Muslims remember him warmly, as a man who knew the earlier scriptures well enough to know what he was hearing.
screen: `A CHRISTIAN WHO KNEW THE SCRIPTURES.` · `COUSIN, LISTEN TO YOUR NEPHEW.` · `THE NAMUS SENT TO MUSA.` · `WILL THEY DRIVE ME OUT?` · then, large: `THE OLD ONES RECOGNIZE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to an elder. Settle, and breathe. Think of the oldest person you know, or the one who's read the most, or lived the most. A grandparent. A neighbor. A retired teacher. Someone at your place of worship. What would you ask them, if you had an hour? Pick one question you actually want the answer to. Picture asking it, and then just listening, without interrupting. If you pray, you can ask Allah to bless your elders. Then, today, ask it. The bell holds the time.
Waraqa the old cousin. Khadijah's elderly, blind cousin, who knew the earlier scriptures and recognized the messenger who came to Musa.
Your line: the old ones recognize. Today, ask one older person your question, and listen to the whole answer. Tomorrow, a silence, and then a surah of morning light. Day eighty-eight.

89.title: The morning brightness
89.hook: after a painful pause in revelation, Surah Ad-Duha comes: your Lord has not forsaken you
89.howItsDone: Surah Ad-Duha is one of the short surahs many Muslims know by heart and recite in times of sadness; some also pray a voluntary prayer called duha in the bright part of the morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Waraqa, the old blind cousin who recognized the messenger of Musa. Your line was the old ones recognize. Did you ask an elder your question? Day eighty-nine.

You know the silence after you send something important. The little word under your text that says delivered, and then nothing. You check. Nothing. You start making up stories: they're angry, I did something wrong, they're gone. After the cave, after iqra, after Waraqa, the revelation stopped. Nothing came. The reports differ on how long, some say days, some much longer. And in Mecca, people noticed. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says a woman mocked him: looks like your companion has abandoned you. Picture how that landed, on a man who had only just stopped shaking.
screen: `DELIVERED. THEN NOTHING.` → `THE REVELATION STOPS.` → `YOUR COMPANION HAS LEFT YOU.`

segments.voice: And then it comes. Surah Ad-Duha, the ninety-third. In Pickthall's translation: “By the morning hours And by the night when it is stillest, Thy Lord hath not forsaken thee nor doth He hate thee.” Ad-duha is the bright part of the morning, when the sun is well up and the day is fully warm. And look how the surah starts. It swears by two things together: the full light of morning, and the still night. As if to say: the night was real. It was quiet. That quiet was not abandonment. The morning comes after it, as sure as the sun. Then it keeps going, gently: what comes later will be better for you than what came before, and your Lord will give you until you are content. And then it reminds him of his own life, the one you've been hearing all week. Did He not find you an orphan, and shelter you? Find you searching, and guide you? Find you in need, and enrich you? Every one of those is a story on this path: Halimah, Abu Talib, Khadijah. You were never left before. You aren't left now. The surah ends by turning the comfort outward: so don't be harsh with the orphan, don't turn away the one who asks, and, in Pickthall's words: “Therefor of the bounty of thy Lord be thy discourse.” Speak of the good you've been given. Many Muslims turn to this surah in the dark stretches of their own lives: after a loss, in depression, when prayer feels like shouting into an empty room. It doesn't deny the night. It swears by it. And then it says: morning.
screen: `BY THE MORNING, BY THE STILL NIGHT.` · `NOT FORSAKEN, NOT HATED.` · `ORPHAN, SEARCHING, IN NEED.` · `OF THE BOUNTY, SPEAK.` · then, large: `YOU HAVE NOT BEEN FORSAKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit in the light for a minute. If it's day, find a window or step outside, and let the light land on your face. If it's night, turn toward a lamp, or just remember the last morning light you felt. Close your eyes. Notice the warmth, or picture it. Then think of one silent stretch in your life that turned out not to be abandonment. If you pray, you can recite the opening: by the morning hours, and by the night when it is stillest. The bell holds the time.
The morning brightness. Ad-Duha, Surah ninety-three, which came after a silence to say: your Lord has not forsaken you.
Your line: you have not been forsaken. Today, send one person who's in a quiet, dark stretch a small sign that they're not forgotten. Tomorrow, the first people who believed. Day eighty-nine.

90.title: The first believers
90.hook: a wife, a boy, a freed slave and a best friend are the first to believe
90.howItsDone: Muslims honor the Prophet's earliest companions and ask Allah to be pleased with them when their names are mentioned; the first believers' stories are taught to children as examples of courage and loyalty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the morning brightness: after a long silence, your Lord has not forsaken you. Your line was you have not been forsaken. Did you send someone a sign? Day ninety.

Every movement you've ever heard of started with a handful of people in a room. Before the crowds, before the history books, there's a kitchen table and three or four people who said yes when saying yes looked a little crazy. Islam started like that. No announcement in the marketplace. No crowd at the Ka'ba. Just a man telling the people closest to him what had happened in the cave, and watching their faces. Who believed first? The answer is four people, and they couldn't be more different.
screen: `A HANDFUL OF PEOPLE IN A ROOM.` → `NO ANNOUNCEMENT, NO CROWD.` → `WHO BELIEVED FIRST?`

segments.voice: First, Khadijah. You already know her. She believed him before there was anything to believe but him. Then 'Ali, his young cousin, Abu Talib's son, a boy of around ten, who had been living in the Prophet's household. Then Zayd ibn Harithah. Zayd had been kidnapped as a child and sold as a slave, and ended up in Khadijah's house, and she gave him to her husband. When Zayd's father finally found him, years later, and came to buy him back, the Prophet ﷺ said: let him choose. And Zayd chose to stay. The Prophet freed him and raised him as a son. And then Abu Bakr, his close friend, a respected merchant. Ibn Ishaq reports that the Prophet said everyone he invited hesitated at least a little, except Abu Bakr, who accepted at once. Abu Bakr then went out and spoke to his own friends, and several of the best-known early Muslims came in through him. Muslims don't all tell the order the same way. Many Sunni scholars say: Khadijah first; among free men, Abu Bakr; among children, 'Ali; among freed slaves, Zayd. Shi'a Muslims emphasize 'Ali as the first male believer. Both honor all four. Look at them together: a wife, a child, a freed slave, a best friend. Not a single powerful man of Quraysh among them. For about three years the community stayed small and quiet, meeting privately, praying in secret. The Qur'an later honors as-sabiqun, the ones who went first, those who believed before it was easy. The first ones matter because they believed when there was nothing to gain.
screen: `KHADIJAH, BEFORE ANYONE.` · `'ALI, A BOY OF TEN.` · `ZAYD, WHO CHOSE TO STAY.` · `ABU BAKR, WITHOUT HESITATING.` · then, large: `THE FIRST ONES MATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the first people who stood with you. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you started: a job, a move, a recovery, a family, a change in yourself. Before it worked, who was there? Say their names, one at a time, silently. Don't rush. Let each face come. Notice if any of them surprise you. Maybe the one who stood with you wasn't the one you expected. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward each of them. The bell holds the time.
The first believers. Khadijah, 'Ali, Zayd and Abu Bakr: a wife, a child, a freed slave and a friend, who believed when it cost something.
Your line: the first ones matter. Today, tell one of your first ones that you remember they were there. Tomorrow, what it cost one early believer. Day ninety.

91.title: Bilal on the hot sand
91.hook: an enslaved man is tortured under a rock in the midday sun, and says only one word: One
91.howItsDone: Muslims honor Bilal as the first mu'adhdhin, and many mosques and schools are named for him; his word, ahad, is remembered as a picture of steadfast tawhid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first believers: a wife, a boy, a freed slave and a friend. Your line was the first ones matter. Did you thank one of yours? Day ninety-one, the end of week thirteen.

Midday in Mecca, in summer. The kind of heat where the sand burns through your sandals. An enslaved man named Bilal is dragged out and laid on his back on that sand. His owner has a huge rock placed on his chest, so he can barely breathe. And the owner says: you'll stay like this until you die, or until you deny Muhammad and worship al-Lat and al-'Uzza. Bilal can't move. He can hardly draw breath. And over and over, all he says is one word. Ahad. Ahad. One. One.
screen: `MIDDAY, BURNING SAND.` → `A ROCK ON HIS CHEST.` → `AHAD. AHAD.`

segments.voice: Bilal ibn Rabah was born into slavery in Mecca; his mother was from Abyssinia, across the Red Sea. His owner, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, was one of the chiefs of Quraysh. The biography by Ibn Ishaq tells the scene you just heard. Why that word? Ahad, One, is the word at the heart of a short surah, the hundred and twelfth, in Pickthall's words: “Say: He is Allah, the One!” Tawhid, day ten of this path, squeezed into a single word by a man who had one breath to spend. It's also a quiet act of defiance. His owner owned his body. He couldn't own that word. And the story doesn't end on the sand. Abu Bakr came by, saw what was being done, and bought Bilal from Umayyah, and set him free. Years later, when the Muslims needed someone to call the people to prayer, it was Bilal's voice they chose. The first adhan, day fifteen of this path, was called by the man who had once said Ahad under a rock. Early Mecca was cruel to the powerless who believed. A woman named Sumayyah, tortured with her family, was killed for her faith; Muslims remember her as the first martyr of Islam. But here's something important. Her son 'Ammar, under torture, said what his tormentors demanded, and came to the Prophet ﷺ in tears. And the Qur'an says that one who is forced, while his heart stays firm in faith, is not blamed. Islam honors Bilal's courage, and it does not demand that everyone be Bilal. That closes week thirteen: a cave, a word, a blanket, an old cousin, the morning light, the first believers, and one word on the burning sand.
screen: `BORN INTO SLAVERY IN MECCA.` · `SAY: HE IS ALLAH, THE ONE!` · `FREED, AND THEN THE FIRST ADHAN.` · `COURAGE HONORED, NOT DEMANDED.` · then, large: `AHAD, AHAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one word of faith under a little pressure. Place your hand flat on your chest and press gently, enough to feel it as you breathe. Now choose one word to hold on to. If you pray, it can be Bilal's word: ahad. One. If not, a word you want to keep when things push on you: steady, or true, or someone's name. Say it silently with each breath, against the gentle weight of your hand. The bell holds the time.
Bilal on the hot sand. An enslaved man, tortured for his faith, who said only Ahad, One, and later called the first adhan.
screen: `BILAL ON THE HOT SAND — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: ahad, ahad. Today, when something presses on you, come back to your one word. Thirteen weeks on the path. Tomorrow, the believers flee across the sea to a just king. Day ninety-one.
